Question
========
How is Linux using free memory to accelerate I/O requests? What happens when the free memory effectively becomes scarce?

Solution
========
Linux uses all otherwise unused memory as a page cache: blocks that are read from disk are kept in memory, and writes are absorbed there and flushed later. This is why free memory on a running Linux is normally close to zero, which is not a problem.

When memory becomes scarce, the kernel reclaims: clean page cache pages are simply dropped, dirty ones must first be written back to the device, and under real pressure anonymous pages get swapped out. Reclaiming is why a burst of allocations can suddenly become slow, and in the worst case the OOM killer terminates a process.
